items.title: Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest
items.summary: Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November, satellite images suggest.
items.content:
Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.

Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.

At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.

The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.

A MAIAR analyst said that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".

Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".

At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.

Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.

At Karaj , external and Shahroud, satellite images appear to show significant excavation. At Karaj, multiple vehicles were visible in satellite images, while improvements appear to have been carried out to the nearby airbase.

The images from Karaj appear to show "a new portal for an underground facility", said Sam Lair, research analyst at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), which has looked extensively into recent developments at Iranian sites.

Analysis from Janes also indicates there appears to be a new facility under construction at Karaj, including tunnel entrances and structures which could indicate an expansion of nearby damaged or destroyed missile bases - or could also be for storage or other purposes.

The construction work is unlikely to be part of an effort to deceive foreign intelligence agencies, said Janes analyst Sean O'Connor. He said such a project "would be costly and may achieve little".

The developments come after repeated assurances from the White House that US-Israeli attacks have depleted the Iranian armed forces, which US President Donald Trump dismissed as a "complete and total mess".

A Pentagon spokesperson previously said that the US had "destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base" and "significantly degraded" the country's ability to launch drone and missile attacks.

But Iran claims it retains large stockpiles of missiles, and footage broadcast on state TV this week claimed to show dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran. Back in August, state TV footage also claimed to show Khordad surface-to-air missiles emerging out of a tunnel near the southern city of Bandar Abbas , external .

A MAIAR analyst also identified new construction and excavations outside tunnel entrances near the city of Qom, close to the Fordo underground uranium enrichment complex, which has been bombed by both the US and Israel multiple times.

Activity related to military assets would show that Tehran is bracing itself for further attacks by the US and Israel, said Mark Cancian, a military analyst with International Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

"The purpose is to better defend itself against future attacks," he said. "It also indicates a priority on rebuilding military capability rather than rehabilitating the economy."

items.title: La nuova sindaca di Los Angeles sarà Nithya Raman, dell’ala socialista dei Democratici
items.content:
La nuova sindaca di Los Angeles sarà Nithya Raman, consigliera comunale che fa parte dell’ala più a sinistra del Partito Democratico. È associata ai Socialisti democratici d’America, il movimento di cui fanno parte anche la celebre deputata Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez e l’attuale sindaco di New York Zohran Mamdani.

Che a Los Angeles avrebbero vinto i Democratici era scontato, ma che Raman avrebbe sconfitto la sindaca Democratica uscente Karen Bass, in carica dal 2022, lo era meno. Raman ha preso il 52 per cento dei voti contro il 48 per cento di Bass, sulla cui sconfitta ha pesato soprattutto la gestione dei disastrosi incendi del gennaio 2025 (i dati non sono definitivi perché lo spoglio non è concluso, ma la vittoria è certa).

Raman rappresenta una nuova generazione di politici Democratici, che contesta l’establishment e propone politiche radicali e attente al concetto di classe. Quest’ala del partito ha avuto ottimi risultati anche alle elezioni di metà mandato , che hanno rinnovato tutti i membri della Camera e un terzo di quelli del Senato, e dove hanno trionfato i Democratici.

Raman ha fatto campagna soprattutto sull’alto costo della vita a Los Angeles e sul diritto alla casa, e ha vinto in particolare tra i giovani. Ha 45 anni, è nata in India, nello stato del Kerala, e vive negli Stati Uniti da quando aveva sei anni. Ha studiato urbanistica e ha fatto la consigliera comunale per cinque anni prima di candidarsi alla carica di sindaca.

items.title: Ci sono davvero hacker filorussi dietro gli attacchi ai frigoriferi dei supermercati?
items.summary: Nella rivendicazione diffusa da due gruppi ci sono alcune cose che non tornano
items.content:
Due gruppi di hacker filorussi, NoName057(16) e Z-Pentest, hanno diffuso un video in cui dicono di essere i responsabili degli attacchi informatici che prima in Francia poi in Italia e in altri paesi europei hanno manomesso frigoriferi e congelatori in decine di supermercati. Rispetto a molti altri casi simili, tuttavia, ci sono alcune cose che non tornano: la mancanza di prove che dimostrino un collegamento diretto agli attacchi sta alimentando dubbi sulle reali intenzioni di questi hacker, non nuovi a operazioni di propaganda.

In Italia sono stati attaccati alcuni supermercati in Sicilia, in Toscana e in provincia di Trento: i frigoriferi hanno smesso di funzionare all’improvviso, la temperatura si è alzata e i responsabili dei punti vendita hanno dovuto buttare molti alimenti ormai guastati. Gli hacker hanno preso di mira il software usato per gestire a distanza i frigoriferi, un sistema pensato per tenere d’occhio i parametri e intervenire rapidamente in caso di anomalie. Nello stesso modo sono stati attaccati supermercati in Belgio, Germania, Irlanda, Paesi Bassi, Portogallo, Estonia, Finlandia e Svezia. A metà ottobre in Francia ne erano stati colpiti circa 700.

Un primo dubbio riguarda la tipologia di attacco, perché NoName057(16) è un gruppo di hacker conosciuto soprattutto per gli attacchi DDoS (Distributed denial of service), che consistono nel mandare a un sito un numero enorme di richieste nel tentativo di sovraccaricarlo e non farlo funzionare. Per compiere un attacco DDoS non serve violare i sistemi di chi viene attaccato. Negli ultimi anni NoName057(16) ha organizzato diversi attacchi in Italia: nel 2025 mandò in tilt il sito della Guardia di Finanza, nel 2024 quello dell’aeroporto di Malpensa .

Z-Pentest invece è stato fondato nel settembre del 2024 da membri di NoName057(16) e di un altro gruppo di hacker, CARR (Cyber Army of Russia Reborn), ed è più specializzato in intrusioni nei sistemi industriali esposti su internet, violati usando password deboli o mai cambiate.

Nel video, pubblicato su Telegram martedì sera, i due gruppi dicono di avere attaccato i sistemi informatici di due marchi del settore della refrigerazione, Danfoss e Dixell, e che lo avrebbero fatto senza usare alcun malware, cioè un software creato appositamente per danneggiare un sistema informatico. Nello stesso video sostengono di poter attaccare reti idriche, centrali elettriche e magazzini alimentari. Poche ore prima NoName057(16) aveva rivendicato un attacco DDoS al sito di Danfoss e aveva pubblicato due file che conterrebbero indirizzi email di clienti e dipendenti dell’azienda.

Una delle anomalie rispetto a casi simili è che né il video né le altre comunicazioni dei due gruppi hacker contengono dettagli utili a confermare l’autenticità della rivendicazione: non dicono quali negozi sono stati attaccati, come sono entrati nei sistemi né quando. Oleg Shakirov, un ricercatore che studia i gruppi di hacker russi, ha notato inoltre che il file originale del video fatto con l’intelligenza artificiale si chiama “хрень”, una parola russa che si può tradurre con “stronzata”.

Diversi altri esperti di sicurezza informatica hanno espresso dubbi sui tempi: gli attacchi più dannosi sono stati compiuti in Francia e risalgono a metà ottobre, ma per settimane nessuno li ha rivendicati, mentre solitamente sia NoName057(16) che Z-Pentest rivendicano subito le loro azioni.

È anche sospetto il modo in cui si è arrivati alla rivendicazione: martedì mattina un canale Telegram di sicurezza informatica, CyberPulse, aveva scritto che gli attacchi ai frigoriferi non erano ancora stati attribuiti a nessuno, ma che il modo in cui erano stati fatti ricordava alcune azioni di Z-Pentest. Poche ore dopo NoName057(16) ha rivendicato l’attacco. Secondo Shakirov è probabile che i gruppi abbiano trovato quell’ipotesi utile e l’abbiano fatta propria, approfittando di una delle notizie di sicurezza informatica più seguite delle ultime settimane.

I dubbi sulla rivendicazione sono condivisi anche dall’Agenzia di cybersicurezza nazionale (ACN): un funzionario ha detto al Post che è presto per capire come sia andata veramente, anche perché non è stato ancora ricostruito come siano stati violati i sistemi, e ha aggiunto che gruppi hacker come NoName057(16) tendono a farsi notare in tutti i modi per dare l’impressione di essere sempre più pericolosi.

Mercoledì il direttore dell’ACN, Andrea Quacivi, è stato sentito dal COPASIR, il comitato parlamentare che controlla i servizi segreti. L’Agenzia di cybersicurezza nazionale ha già invitato le aziende della grande distribuzione a migliorare la sicurezza dei sistemi informatici, perché gli attacchi di questi giorni sono stati favoriti dalla presenza di software non aggiornati o non più aggiornabili perché fuori mercato.

items.title: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
items.summary: Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state".
items.content:
Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.

Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.

His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".

Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.

The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.

Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".

These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.

Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.

He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".

Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.

Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.

"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.

Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.

Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.

These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.

Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail . Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

items.title: In Sudafrica l’ANC ha perso le grandi città
items.summary: Il partito che fu di Nelson Mandela è crollato in quasi tutte le aree metropolitane più importanti, un segnale molto negativo
items.content:
Alle elezioni locali in Sudafrica lo spoglio non è ancora concluso, ma un risultato è già evidente: il Congresso nazionale africano (ANC), lo storico partito di centrosinistra che fu di Nelson Mandela e che governa dagli anni Novanta, perderà quasi tutte le città più grandi e importanti del paese. Si votava per rinnovare le amministrazioni di oltre 250 comuni, e l’ANC è andato molto male in quasi tutte le principali aree metropolitane.

A scrutinio inoltrato nella capitale Pretoria l’ANC ha preso circa il 21 per cento, contro il 32 di Alleanza Democratica (AD), il partito liberale con una base elettorale prevalentemente bianca con cui l’ANC governa in coalizione dal 2024. È quindi addirittura il terzo partito, dopo ActionSA, di centrodestra, con il 24 per cento.

A Città del Capo l’ANC ha preso appena il 9,7 per cento, stando alle schede scrutinate, contro il 60 per cento di Alleanza Democratica. A Johannesburg il 17 per cento contro il 40 di AD. Al momento tra le grandi città è in testa solo a Buffalo City, nel sudest.

A livello nazionale l’ANC dovrebbe prendere tra il 30 e il 35 per cento: il risultato peggiore della sua storia. Alle precedenti amministrative, nel 2021, prese il 46. Non è un caso che l’ANC abbia perso soprattutto nelle città, dove i problemi più pressanti per i sudafricani sono evidenti: criminalità diffusa e infrastrutture decadenti che portano spesso a interruzioni nell’erogazione dell’acqua e della corrente elettrica.

Che avrebbe ottenuto un pessimo risultato era previsto: è in crisi di consensi da tempo e ha fatto una campagna elettorale pigra e in ritardo. Perdere nelle grandi città ha anche un valore politico rilevante, perché sono i luoghi dove si decide il futuro politico del paese.

Le elezioni legislative del 2024 mostrarono in modo evidente la disaffezione dell’elettorato verso il partito. Furono le prime in cui l’ANC non uscì vincitore assoluto e dovette formare un’alleanza, peraltro dal forte valore simbolico: l’ANC è il partito che lottò per la fine dell’apartheid, il regime di violenta segregazione razziale in vigore in Sudafrica per buona parte del Novecento; AD è l’erede del Partito Progressista, il partito liberale che contestò l’apartheid, ma dentro vi confluirono anche molti ex elettori e dirigenti del Partito Nazionale, cioè il partito nazionalista afrikaner che nel 1948 istituzionalizzò la segregazione (un’altra parte finì poi nella stessa ANC, quando nel 2005 il Partito Nazionale si sciolse).

Lo schema di quelle elezioni nazionali si è ripetuto alle amministrative, e in alcuni casi per l’ANC è andata pure peggio: non solo governerà in coalizione, ma in molti casi sarà il partito di minoranza. La ragione di questo crollo è in parte generazionale: se per le vecchie generazioni l’ANC ha rappresentato un simbolo della lotta per la liberazione dei sudafricani neri, oggi per molti giovani che non hanno vissuto l’apartheid è solo un partito vecchio e clientelare e che spesso amministra i territori in modo inefficace.

items.title: Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results?
items.summary: BBC Verify examines whether US voters were influenced by the data centre boom - and the impact anti-AI sentiment could have on the industry.
items.content:
A US midterms voter poll has suggested data centres were a highly motivating issue for many Americans, leading some to argue public backlash against the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure construction boom might have helped shape the election outcome.

BBC Verify has looked at its role in the campaign and examined the potential consequences for the AI industry.

The poll for AP and a consortium of news organisations found 56% of surveyed voters said data centres were a "crucial or major" factor in their vote, while 76% said they would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.

The hostile sentiment was considerably stronger among those who said they voted Democrat at this election.

This follows other recent Pew Research polling , external which suggested about half of Americans think data centres are "mostly bad" for the environment, home energy costs and quality of life, a big deterioration in favourability since January.

The congressional voter poll results certainly suggest a remarkable degree of salience for a subject which likely would not have been on most Americans' radar five years ago.

However, it is some way behind several key issues people considered a "crucial or major factor" in their vote, including government corruption (90%) and the cost of living (89%).

Three of the Senate seats flipped by the Democrats have significantly more data centres , external , Texas (595), Ohio (258) and Iowa (117), than the median of 55 across all 50 states.

And Texas alone has 31 ongoing data centre construction projects, the most of any state , external .

But other factors would also have been motivating voters in these states, as elsewhere.

BBC Verify analysis of state-level voter polling for Senate elections suggests states which swung to the Democrats either followed the national trend over data centre concerns, or seemed less concerned.

So we can't say how many votes or Senate seats were directly delivered by data centre opposition.

But it's notable that three key states in the US AI build-out, Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all elected Democrats as senators and governors who called for tighter regulation on data centres in one form or another.

requirements to fully cover their own energy and water infrastructure costs

The US economy has been heavily supported in recent years by massive corporate investments in AI , external , including for data centre construction.

Official data , external shows inflation-adjusted monthly spending on building data centres, excluding the IT hardware to go into them, in August 2026 was $5bn (£4.2bn) - five times higher than in 2023.

Analysis by Columbia Business School , external suggests AI infrastructure investment in the US is currently larger as a share of the overall economy than spending on new railways was at the height of that boom in the 19th Century.

Cori Crider, executive director of the Future of Tech Institute, a European think tank, told BBC Verify the industry should anticipate that new state leaders will put conditions on or "even stop runaway data centre build".

Seema Shah, from global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said requirements for developers to pay for additional investment in the electricity grid, meet tougher standards over their usage of resources like water, or give up tax incentives could "raise development costs and slow new supply".

However, Heather West from the Eurasia Group consultancy said temporary bans on construction and new regulations might delay the data centre roll out, but would not stop it entirely.

She said "projects already permitted or under construction will largely proceed", but delays would affect the "next wave" of building through "local fights, slower permitting, and pressure to make data centres pay for their own power".

Analysts from the consultancy Oxford Economics have said there are also strong economic incentives for politicians to avoid policies that would severely disrupt data centre construction, pointing to tax revenue and construction jobs they bring.

Deepak Surana of the Futurum Group, a technology research firm, said he expected there would ultimately be "a negotiation, not a moratorium" from Texas state leaders on data centres to ensure no negative impact on residents' energy and water bills.

OpenAI, which has a data centre in Texas and under-construction projects in Ohio, pledged to ensure it fully paid for its own electricity on Thursday , external - one day after the midterm results.

Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett, Rob England and Christine Jeavans

items.title: A wildfire killed their loved ones in Spain. These British families demand to know why
items.summary: Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the village of Bédar this summer.
items.content:
Relatives of Britons killed in this summer's wildfires in Spain have told the BBC they are disgusted, after regional politicians blocked an official inquiry into the disaster.

Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the hillside village of Bédar, in the province of Almería in south-eastern Spain, on 9 July.

Families have criticised the authorities' actions, including the decision not to send an emergency alert to mobile phones as the flames closed in.

"If that evacuation warning had come through in time, my father would still be alive," says Duncan Chard, who blames failures by officials on the day for a number of the deaths.

The governing People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox in the Andalusian parliament have rejected a request for a commission of inquiry made by the opposition Socialist party to which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez belongs.

The PP and Vox argued that an ongoing criminal investigation would provide the necessary answers.

The Andalusian government, PP and Vox have been approached for comment.

Families of those killed say there must be a public and transparent probe.

"It's just outrageous. It's an injustice. As family members, we're absolutely disgusted. This is an insult," says Duncan Chard.

The families also say their grief has been made worse by how police have handled their loved ones' remains and belongings since the fire.

Michael Chard built his house in Bédar from scratch. "He called it Casa Micas," his son said. "It was his place in the sun, it was his little paradise."

On the morning of the fire, Michael's partner Christine had met friends and was due to go to the hairdresser. "Then everything changed... the whole world changed for them," he said.

Duncan Chard said his father, who had two artificial knees and walked with a stick, left his house with Christine as soon as they saw the flames. They left their phones and passports behind and tried to escape by car, but the road was blocked.

"This is an action of a brave person who was fighting to the end," he said.

Andalusia's emergencies chief, Antonio Sanz, has said the region decided not to use the system that sends emergency alerts to mobile phones because it could not be tailored to specific communities.

Officials have said some residents needed to evacuate while others were safer staying in their homes. They also argued an alert could have caused panic and traffic jams.

"Issue the damned alert!" said Chard. "Ring the bells, send the police guy out with his horn, go door to door, do everything."

Thomas-Wolf Verdonckt, a Belgian virologist whose father Stanislas, 63, died, was on the phone to him as the flames approached.

He says the victims "never received advice on what they should do, and certainly not warnings that they were in danger", and that the authorities' claim that everyone in the area was given adequate warning is not true.

"The only contact that the government managed to make with the victims was a couple of minutes before the flames engulfed everyone. One police car drove by with the sirens on. There was no talking, there was no messaging."

Bédar's emergency plan was last approved in 2019, and regional officials say it was in the process of being updated. The municipality is classified by the Andalusian government as being at risk from wildfires.

Of the 15 people who died in Bédar, 14 were foreign nationals: nine British citizens, three Belgian, one French and one American. The other victim was Spanish.

In the days after the fire, Sanz faced a backlash for appearing to blame the victims. He said some people who made the decision to leave "at the last minute, took the wrong path".

Verdonckt has been trying to find answers ever since the blaze.

"The morning afterwards, the Spanish officials brought out... a version of events which was simply the complete opposite of what I experienced," he said.

He also believes a public inquiry is needed to prevent a similar disaster happening in Spain in the future.

"They are putting the safety of citizens in second place. That's simply not okay."

Danni Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, lost her parents Pete and Fran in the fire.

They had lived in Bédar since 2018. Fran, a former headteacher, ran a quiz night that raised money for the local school and church.

"They were fantastic parents, my biggest champions and cheerleaders," said Danni. "They leave a huge, huge hole in our lives."

She says her mother texted her at about 19:00 to say they had packed in case they had to leave.

"They were waiting for instructions, and those instructions didn't come," she said.

Her parents died on the part of Bédar known as English Hill, one of the places where, families say, the authorities' only contact came minutes before the flames arrived.

Gillam-Kirton says her grief has been made worse by the way the Spanish authorities have behaved since.

Local police had told the family that Pete and Fran's car had been "meticulously searched" by forensic specialists and that she would find nothing.

But in August, a month afterwards, Gillam-Kirton and her husband found what appeared to be human bones in the burnt-out car in which her father died. "I picked up what I recognised to be... part of a pelvis or a hip joint," she said.

Within minutes they also found her parents' mobile phones, jewellery, house keys and money. Police had earlier told the family that no personal belongings had survived.

Spain's Guardia Civil police have been approached for comment.

The fragments were eventually sent to Madrid for testing. The family says police have now told them no DNA was recovered and that the bones were those of an animal.

But Gillam-Kirton says experts, including a forensic anthropologist who worked on the Grenfell Tower fire investigation, believe the fragments were human.

Gillam-Kirton complained to the Guardia Civil. She says the reply told her only that the matter had been passed to the courts, and offered condolences for "the death of your relative", in the singular, when in fact she had lost both her parents.

"It feels like they're going to hope that we exhaust ourselves," she said. "Either the burden of grief is going to be enough for us to give up, or that we're going to financially exhaust ourselves."

Gillam-Kirton says there is "a real lack of empathy when you're dealing with families that have lost so much".

The one thing she wants above all is for someone to acknowledge what went wrong: "No-one seems to be willing to say 'do you know what, we made a mistake and for that we are sorry'."

The death toll in Bédar was the highest from any single fire in Spain during the summer of 2026, and one of the largest in the country's history.

Many victims were trapped as they tried to escape the village, as survivor Malcolm Timbrell told me outside his devastated home in July.

The cause of the disaster, also known as the Los Gallardos fire after the neighbouring town where it started, is the subject of a criminal investigation.

In July, the Guardia Civil said it was believed to have been started by a fallen power line, but that explanation has been called into question.

The BBC has seen a letter in which the Andalusian government refused a request from Socialist MPs for its official reports on the fire. These included any documents explaining why no alert was sent to mobile phones.

The letter, signed by Sanz in September, said the documents could not be released because the criminal investigation is under secreto de sumario , a court order keeping the case file confidential.

Gillam-Kirton says the criminal case is focused on how the fire started, and that it will not necessarily examine the emergency response unless families pay lawyers to put that evidence before the judge.

"How can you have faith in these measures that they're putting in to mitigate future disasters if you don't know fully what happened the first time around?" she said.

"That's why you have a public inquiry," said Duncan Chard, "because the public need answers."

Families in the UK, Belgium and Spain have set up various support groups, as well as a website called helpbedar.com.

They have launched an appeal to pay for legal action, aiming to raise €100,000 (£83,000). Fundraising events are being held in both Spain and the UK, and so far about €11,000 has been collected.

"We are getting steamrolled by the Andalusian government," said Chard.

Ultimately, the families say all they want is answers, and for lessons to be learned so that others do not suffer the same ordeal.

They say they want their fight to be a tribute to their loved ones who died.

"I feel like this is all I can do for them," said Gillam-Kirton.

Wildfire in southern Spain leaves at least 12 dead and 23 missing

items.title: I robot cinesi per produrre, non solo per stupire: Pudu spinge sul mercato europeo
items.summary: Dieci anni fa era una startup di Shenzhen, oggi è il primo produttore al mondo di robot di servizio commerciali e ha nell'Europa il suo primo mercato. Ad Amsterdam Pudu ha mostrato tutta la gamma, dai robot per le pulizie agli umanoidi. Il fondatore Felix Zhang ha giocato.a tutto campo parlando di ascensori, posti di lavoro e robot in casa. ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Nata nel 2016 nel cuore pulsante di Shenzhen da un'idea dell'ingegnere Felix Zhang, che ha condotto la conferenza stampa di Amsterdam, Pudu Robotics incarna la parabola di come un piccolo laboratorio di automazione possa trasformarsi, nel giro di pochi anni, in un attore globale della robotica commerciale.

Nei primi anni di vita, l'azienda ha intercettato una necessità concreta quanto trascurata: sollevare il personale della ristorazione dalle mansioni più ripetitive della sala. I robot camerieri (non si pensi a umanoidi ma a carrelli attrezzati e autonomi) hanno preso velocemente piede sul mercato, ma il vero punto di svolta è arrivato nel 2019 con l'introduzione di BellaBot, un dispositivo da consegna che affianca alla navigazione autonoma un'interfaccia espressiva dalle sembianze feline, capace di mitigare la naturale diffidenza delle persone verso le macchine negli spazi pubblici. Sostenuta da imponenti investimenti di grandi gruppi come Tencent e Meituan, Pudu ha progressivamente esteso il proprio raggio d'azione, passando dai vassoi delle sale da pranzo ai macchinari per la pulizia industriale negli aeroporti e, più recentemente, allo sviluppo di piattaforme di "intelligenza artificiale incarnata", così la chiama l'azienda. Si tratta di una piattaforma di AI centralizzata che può governare in maniera coordinata una flotta di robot più o meno eterogenei, garantendo un approccio coerente su tutte le applicazioni robotiche.

Oggi, con oltre 130.000 robot spediti in più di 85 Paesi, tra cui molte applicazioni già operative in Europa, Pudu ha deciso di penetrare il nostro continente in maniera più completa, con l'apertura di un magazzino con prodotti finiti e tutte le parti di ricambio nei Paesi Bassi e la già citata filiale in Germania.

Il dato che sorprende di più arriva quasi di sfuggita, durante la presentazione di Zhang: oltre l'80% del fatturato di Pudu viene da fuori della Cina, e il primo mercato in assoluto è l'Europa. Non è un caso, quindi, che l'azienda abbia scelto Amsterdam per il suo primo European Partner Summit, l'evento in cui ha mostrato per la prima volta tutte e sei le sue linee di prodotto insieme. Secondo l'azienda, negli ultimi due anni il fatturato europeo è cresciuto in media di oltre il 60% l'anno, con una presenza in più di 20 Paesi, Italia compresa.

A guidare l'operazione europea è Bella Sun, vicepresidente e responsabile per l'Europa, che ha messo l'accento più sull'assistenza che sulle vendite.

" Vendere un robot è una cosa, farlo funzionare bene ogni giorno presso il cliente è un'altra ", ha detto. Da qui l'hub di Neuss, vicino a Düsseldorf, inaugurato a fine ottobre: uffici, showroom, centro di formazione, laboratorio di riparazione e magazzino ricambi sotto lo stesso tetto. In Europa lavorano circa 50 commerciali e una quarantina di tecnici dell'assistenza.

Ad Amsterdam i robot erano tutti esposti, e a guardarli da vicino si capisce subito che sono macchine da lavoro. Nessuno fa capriole: ognuno ha un compito preciso e un cliente che lo paga per svolgerlo. Il catalogo oggi conta sei linee di prodotto.

I robot "camerieri" e "fattorini" sono quelli da cui tutto è partito. Il PuduBot del 2016 e il suo erede PuduBot 2 sono di fatto carrelli a ripiani che vanno da soli dalla cucina al tavolo.

BellaBot, nella nuova versione Pro, aggiunge il famoso muso da gatto, l'interazione vocale e la capacità di muoversi in passaggi larghi appena 65 centimetri, utile nei locali affollati.

Il robot può essere utilizzato, per esempio, per portare dei piatti appena preparati al tavolo che li ha ordinati o per riportare verso la cucina i piatti dopo la consumazione. Ogni ripiano è inquadrato da una telecamera così da rendere il robot consapevole se il piatto è ancora sul vassoio o meno.

FlashBot e SwiftBot sono invece armadietti chiusi su ruote, pensati per portare oggetti nelle camere d'albergo, negli ospedali o tra i piani di un ufficio, prendendo l'ascensore. Secondo l'azienda, la catena di ristoranti giapponese Skylark usa più di 3.000 robot Pudu.

I robot per le pulizie - un po' come accade a casa - sono oggi il prodotto di punta, soprattutto nei supermercati europei.

Il CC1 è una sorta di aspirapolvere-lavapavimenti autonomo che in una sola passata spazza, lava, aspira e asciuga. Nella versione Pro rileva in tempo reale se il pavimento è rimasto sporco e ci ripassa. È il modello che Denner ha installato in oltre 200 esemplari nei suoi supermercati svizzeri, con un consumo d'acqua ridotto dell'85%, secondo l'azienda.

L'MT1 è invece una spazzatrice per lo sporco asciutto, con un contenitore da 30 litri che svuota da solo in una stazione dedicata.

Per i grandi spazi, come magazzini e centri commerciali, c'è il BG1, una lavasciuga autonoma di grandi dimensioni.

Ci sono poi i robot per la logistica industriale : sono probabilmente i meno spettacolari e i più concreti.

La serie T è una famiglia di carrelli autonomi che spostano merci e componenti tra reparti e magazzini: il T150 porta fino a 150 chili, il T300 fino a 300, il T600 fino a 600. Quest'ultimo esiste anche in versione "underride", bassa, che si infila sotto uno scaffale, lo solleva e lo porta dove serve.

Per carichi ancora più pesanti, c'è il nuovo MP2000, un trasportatore di pallet fino a 2.000 chili: riconosce il carico da solo, allinea le forche e le inserisce in una ventina di secondi.

La famiglia "embodied AI", letteralmente "AI incarnata", è quella che più si avvicina all'immaginario dei robot con richiami alla fantascienza, ma anche qui l'approccio è pratico.

Il D5 è il tipico cane-robot quadrupede, proposto alla conferenza stampa nella più convincente versione con ruote al posto dei piedi, pensato per ispezioni in impianti energetici, data center e siti industriali.

Nella versione a ruote (che sono comunque applicate a degli arti che permettono di salire i gradini o superare ostacoli), il robot raggiunge velocità di spostamento fino a 5 m/s, circa 18 km/h, molto di più del passo camminato delle versioni "a zampe". Il cane è pensato per ospitare sul "groppone" una serie di sensori specializzati, a seconda dell'uso, come camere termiche o rilevatori 3D.

Il D7 è un semi-umanoide: busto e due braccia su una base a ruote, per lavori di manipolazione come prendere e posare oggetti: il vantaggio di avere le "braccia" senza la complicazione di stare in equilibrio sulle gambe. Non manca (anche se non esposto ad Amsterdam) l'umanoide bipede vero e proprio, il D9.

I rasaerba professionali della serie GT sono l'ultima famiglia professionale, lanciata a settembre scorso. Il GT3 è compatto e pensato per aree verdi piccole e frammentate, come quelle di ospedali, campus e parchi aziendali.

Il GT5 taglia una fascia di 152 cm e raccoglie l'erba, per grandi superfici. Il GT7 è un tosaerba a lame elicoidali per campi da golf e campi sportivi, dove la qualità del taglio conta più di tutto. Il sesto prodotto, il rasaerba domestico TOMO S, è il primo pensato per le famiglie: ne parliamo in fondo.

A tenere insieme tutto c'è quella che l'azienda chiama strategia "One Brain, Multiple Embodiments", un cervello e tanti corpi. In pratica, tutti i robot condividono lo stesso modello fondazionale (PuduFM) e la stessa piattaforma software (PuduAgent OS): le abilità sviluppate per un robot possono essere riusate su un altro, mentre l'hardware resta progettato per il suo compito specifico. Pudu dice di addestrare il modello con i dati raccolti dai robot già installati, circa 50 milioni di ore di lavoro reale all'anno.

Dietro la formula c'è soprattutto una ragione economica, e Zhang non l'ha nascosta: sviluppare un nuovo modello di robot costa di solito oltre 6 milioni di euro. Condividere software e componenti tra prodotti diversi abbassa i costi e accorcia i tempi di progettazione e sviluppo. E c'è l'argomento commerciale: " Un hotel ha bisogno di robot per il ristorante, per il servizio in camera, per pulire i piani e il parcheggio ", ha spiegato Zhang. " Se deve rivolgersi a quattro fornitori diversi, con quattro cloud e quattro assistenze diverse, è un incubo ". Vero. Ma va anche detto che a volte si scelgono fornitori e piattaforme diversi a seconda degli impieghi per avere una maggiore flessibilità di sostituzione parziale quando le cose non dovessero funzionare come ci si aspetta.

Alla domanda su cosa sappiano già fare i robot Pudu che potrebbe sorprendere il pubblico, Zhang ha risposto con tre esempi molto terra terra. Il primo è quasi un gioco: se si toccano le orecchie di BellaBot, il robot-cameriere dalla faccia di gatto, risponde con un verso felino, contento o seccato. Piace moltissimo, ha raccontato, e la gente lo tocca apposta. E no, il nome non viene da Bella Sun: il robot è arrivato prima di lei in azienda.

Il secondo è più interessante. I pavimenti veri hanno sporco asciutto e sporco bagnato, e i robot di Pudu si dividono il lavoro. Se la spazzatrice MT1 trova una pozza d'acqua, chiama il CC1 per lavarla; se il CC1, che lava, incontra rifiuti asciutti, chiama l'MT1 per spazzarli. Il terzo è la stazione di svuotamento automatico dell'MT1: quando il contenitore da 30 litri è pieno, il robot va da solo a svuotarlo e riprende il giro, così può coprire superfici molto grandi senza qualcuno che lo segua.

items.title: Trump ha dichiarato lo Studio Ovale monumento nazionale, ma i suoi successori potranno ancora modificarlo
items.content:
Il presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump ha firmato un provvedimento per dichiarare monumento nazionale lo Studio Ovale, l’ufficio presidenziale della Casa Bianca a Washington, e la Cabinet Room, la stanza dove si riunisce il governo. Trump ha detto che l’obiettivo è impedire ai suoi successori di modificare o demolire questi ambienti: «Non sarà permesso a nessuno di toccarli», ha detto.

Durante il suo secondo mandato Trump ha modificato profondamente gli ambienti della Casa Bianca, aggiungendo molte decorazioni dorate nello Studio Ovale, con uno stile opulento in netto contrasto con quello dei suoi predecessori.

Il provvedimento, però, non impedisce ai futuri presidenti di cambiare l’arredamento e non esclude che possano revocarlo. Prevede che prima di interventi sostanziali sulla struttura siano documentate e valutate possibili alternative, ma non impone che debbano essere autorizzati dal Congresso, come invece ha sostenuto Trump.

items.title: Leo XIV in Latin America: a confrontation with the right
items.summary: The Pope departs today and returns on 17 November. No special medical precautions are needed following his operation on 13 October. Vatican communications chief Montse Alvarado: “He is doing well.” In Buenos Aires, Milei and Peter Thiel await him; in Lima, the daughter of Alberto Fujimori
items.content:
It is a homecoming. It is a stress test for his pontificate following his recent lung operation. And it is a journey into a region that is both a religious stronghold — Latin America is home to the largest share of the world's Catholics — and a politically turbulent landscape.

These are the three defining themes of Pope Leo XIV’s visit to Uruguay, Peru and Argentina, which begins today and runs until 17 November.

Over 12 days, Robert Francis Prevost will travel more than 30,000 kilometres, visit 14 locations, take numerous flights by plane and helicopter, attend more than 50 engagements and deliver around 40 speeches.

It is a demanding, tightly packed schedule that Leo XIV was determined not to alter after undergoing successful surgery on 13 October to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.

The Pope himself wanted the operation scheduled in time for the trip, which had already been arranged. After being discharged from Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, he gradually resumed work and public appearances, although he did forgo some engagements, including a helicopter trip to Assisi.

Only after receiving favourable test results and clearance from his doctors did the Holy See confirm, on 26 October, that the Pontiff would indeed make the journey “according to the previously published programme”.

All the stops have therefore been confirmed, including those that had caused some concern even among Latin American cardinals, such as the visit to Cuzco, Peru, an Indigenous city situated more than 3,000 metres above sea level.

“The plan remains unchanged,” Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni told a briefing, appearing alongside Montse Alvarado, the young Mexican-born American who has headed the Vatican’s communications department since 1 November.

“Ordinary medical care is considered sufficient,” Bruni said, explaining that there would be “no special arrangements or equipment”.

“The Pope has fantastic stamina,” Alvarado added. “You saw him at Mass yesterday. He sings in a way that you can only sing if you have very strong lungs. The Pope is grateful for the concern and affection. We have everything we need, but the doctors are very confident and he is in excellent health.”

As on previous trips, the Pope will be accompanied by his personal physician, Luigi Carboni, and nurses, while an ambulance will also be part of the entourage.

“I am happy to be returning to the continent where I spent so many moments of my life,” the Pope said.

Born in Chicago 71 years ago, Robert Francis Prevost spent more than 20 years of his life in northern Peru, first as a young missionary — in Chulucanas in 1985, then in Trujillo from 1988 to 1999 — and later as bishop of Chiclayo, from 2014 to 2023. As superior general of the Augustinian order from 2001 to 2013, he also visited several Latin American countries, including Argentina, where he met the then archbishop of Buenos Aires, Jorge Mario Bergoglio, with whom he initially had some disagreements.

After becoming Pope, Francis appointed him first as a bishop in Peru and later brought him to Rome to head the Vatican department responsible for selecting bishops around the world. Francis never concealed his fondness for this “American, yes, but from the south”, as he liked to put it.

Latin America is home to 575 million Catholics, more than 40% of the worldwide total. According to figures from the Pew Research Center, however, the proportion of people identifying as Catholic has declined over the past decade, while the number of non-believers has risen. Evangelical Protestantism, meanwhile, has been growing for decades.

Politically, the region has seen many governments shift to the right in recent months.

Apart from the recent victory of Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva in Brazil, relatively few countries are now governed by left-wing politicians — Mexico, Guatemala, Guyana, Suriname, Uruguay and Cuba — while the radical and populist right has come to power in many others, including Ecuador, Colombia, Bolivia, Honduras, Chile, Costa Rica and Peru, as well as Argentina before them.

“May this journey be an opportunity to open our hearts to one another,” the Pope said, “strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy!”

Pope Leo begins his visit in Uruguay, Latin America’s most secularised country, with a history also marked by a degree of anticlericalism. So much so that, as Vatican News recently recalled, Christmas is known as Family Day and Holy Week as Tourism Week. Welcomed by the left-wing president Yamandú Orsi, the Pope will spend 48 hours in the country, visiting both the capital, Montevideo, and Paysandú, where he will celebrate Mass among rural communities on Saturday, 7 November. As well as meeting government officials, bishops and representatives of Uruguayan society, he will visit the Catholic university and preside over an evening vigil at the capital’s stadium.

The second leg of the journey, from Sunday to Wednesday, takes the Pope to Argentina. It is the homeland of Jorge Mario Bergoglio, who never returned to his native country as Pope, prompting questions and some resentment.

That is one more reason why Argentine Catholics are eagerly awaiting the visit: they have not welcomed a Pope to their country since John Paul II travelled there in 1987.

Leo will be greeted by President Javier Milei, a figure of the far right who initially insulted Francis, accusing him of being a “communist” and an “imbecile”.

Once in office, however, Milei repaired relations with the Pope. Francis welcomed him with open arms because, as La Nación put it, “you have to plough with the oxen you have”.

Milei’s policies dismantling the welfare state in recent years have increased poverty and inequality, drawing open criticism from the Argentine Catholic Church.

For this reason, the government has organised the visit amid concerns that Leo might raise issues or meet people who could amplify those criticisms.

Milei has embraced its development, announcing his intention not to regulate it, while in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, Leo strongly calls for regulation and warns of the risks.

Peter Thiel, one of the leading figures of the American tech right, has also recently moved to Buenos Aires.

Obsessed with the figure of the Antichrist, Thiel has described Leo as a “woke pope” and a “useful idiot” of the Chinese communist government.

In Argentina, Leo will visit Buenos Aires, Córdoba, in the east of the country, and Luján, near the capital, home to a famous Marian shrine.

His public engagements reflect the diversity of Argentine society and the Church.

Among other things, Leo will visit the “Little Cottolengo”, a facility caring for people with disabilities and those struggling with drug addictions.

He will also meet representatives of business, trade unions and grassroots movements, whom he has already received at the Vatican, on Monday.

On Tuesday, he will preside over a vigil with young people at the Monumento de los Españoles, before visiting a prison on Wednesday.

Although it is smaller than Argentina, the Pope will spend six days there.

He will be welcomed by the new president, Keiko Fujimori, daughter of former president and dictator Alberto Fujimori, who ruled the country from 1990 to 2000 using increasingly authoritarian methods.

As reconstructed by both Elise Allen, in the only book-length interview with the Pope, and Daniel Burke and Scott Detrow in their biography, Prevost remained in Peru as a missionary despite death threats against American priests from the left-wing terrorist movement Shining Path.

At the same time, he quietly encouraged petitions and demonstrations against human rights violations committed by the Fujimori regime.

The new president, who took office only a few months ago, has announced a military-led security crackdown to combat drug cartels and the criminal networks surrounding them.

Another emergency is looming over the country: El Niño, the exceptional weather phenomenon that threatens floods, droughts and major disruption to the fishing industry.

For the Pope, returning to Peru means coming home and offering the world a tangible expression of his vision of a Church committed to society’s most vulnerable.

Alongside numerous meetings with political and Church representatives, Prevost will attend a gathering in Lima on “the challenges and hopes for the future of the Peruvian people”, together with his friend Cardinal Carlos Castillo.

He will meet young people and university students at the capital’s stadium, fly to the open-air site of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, travel up into the highlands to the Indigenous city of Cuzco and reach Pucallpa, on the edge of the Amazon rainforest.

Above all, he will return to Chiclayo, the diocese where he served as bishop for ten years.

Initially, he had to contend with a hostile environment heavily dominated by Opus Dei.

He recalled Chiclayo from the balcony of St Peter’s Basilica on the very evening of his election, after the white smoke had announced the choice of a new Pope.

items.title: From the Colosseum to the Sabina hills: a taste of Lazio’s olive oil
items.summary: Explore Rome and its countryside through olive oil tastings, historic mills and the Evo Experience, a journey into one of the region’s most treasured food traditions
items.content:
ROMA – All roads lead to Rome. But this time, the journey begins in the heart of the Eternal City and leads out into the olive groves of Lazio. And the starting point is a surprising one: the Colosseum.

Best known for its ancient ruins, the Colosseum Archaeological Park also encompasses the Roman Forum and Palatine Hill, with more than 40 hectares of green space in the heart of Rome. Here, visitors can explore trails dedicated to olive oil, wine and even honey. It is the first stop on a journey through the region’s olive oil traditions, from the capital to the historic mills of Sabina.

The park is home to 189 olive trees of different ages, growing along the Via Sacra, on the slopes of the Palatine Hill and near the Arch of Titus. Among them, the younger Leccino trees produce an olive oil called Palatinum, intended primarily for cultural and institutional use rather than commercial sale.

“Looking after the olive trees and producing Palatinum are central to our partnership with Coldiretti Lazio,” explains Simone Quilici, director of the Colosseum Archaeological Park. “OP Latium and Unaprol are also involved in managing the agricultural activities. The project allows us to put the olives to good use while preserving and celebrating a botanical heritage that is an integral part of the site's history.”

From olive oil to wine is only a short step – at least within the park. In recent years, the Barberini vineyard on the Palatine Hill has been brought back to life. Its ancient indigenous grape variety, known to Pliny the Elder as uva pantastica , is the source of Bellone, a wine produced under the Parco Green project in the shadow of the Colosseum.

Since 2022, this “noble vineyard” has been part of Iter Vitis, one of the Council of Europe's Cultural Routes, an initiative designed to promote and safeguard Europe's tangible and intangible wine-growing heritage.

Just a short walk away, along a path winding through the hill's Mediterranean vegetation, visitors will find the beehives that produce Ambrosia del Palatino, honey made by Rome's own bees.

Beyond the historic centre, Rome's own olive trees – the ulivi de' noantri , as locals might call them – offer further opportunities to explore the city's olive oil heritage.

One such trail runs through Parco dei Romanisti, in the Torrespaccata neighbourhood, where the city authorities have been giving a new lease of life to olive trees removed from Viale Mazzini, in the Prati district, as well as those growing at Villa Glori.

In May 2025, 13 olive trees were planted in the green space along Via dei Romanisti, joining the 35 already there. The transplanted trees had originally formed part of the tree-lined landscape of Viale Mazzini, which has since been redeveloped in keeping with the original design by Raffaele De Vico – a plan that did not include olive trees.

The trees have found a new home in a public space where local residents play an active role. In the park, the Gaspar8 association runs an olive-harvesting and oil-production project, with the aim of donating the resulting oil to families in need.

The park's collection of trees continues to grow: in early 2026, the association planted a further 17 olive trees.

“The aim of the project – carried out entirely by local residents on a voluntary, unpaid basis – is both environmental and social,” explains Sabrina Alfonsi, Rome's councillor for agriculture, the environment and waste management.

The city's historic villas also offer opportunities to discover olive oil trails that combine environmental regeneration, landscape restoration and agricultural heritage. At Villa Glori, a project is under way to restore the park's 400 olive trees.

Another highlight is Rome's own municipal olive oil, produced at the Castel di Guido agricultural estate, just a few kilometres from the capital. The oil has been awarded Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) status, an EU quality label granted to products whose characteristics are linked to their place of origin. The November olive harvest is now under way, and everyone is welcome to take part.

November is the perfect month to discover Italy's olive oil culture at first hand. Olive mills are in full swing, opening their doors for tours and tastings. Freshly harvested olives are pressed into oil, then drizzled over slices of warm bread, releasing fresh, grassy aromas and distinctive bitter and peppery notes.

Lazio's olive oil industry is enjoying growing success, with production figures and recognition on the rise. Extra virgin olive oil (EVO) is far more than an agricultural product: it is an expression of local identity and an important part of the region's cultural heritage.

Across the Agro Pontino, Sabina, Tuscia and the Castelli Romani, numerous initiatives invite visitors to discover the different stages of production, explore olive groves and take part in guided tastings.

Among the most interesting destinations is Sonnino, in the province of Latina. At this time of year, visitors can explore the Cetrone family estate and olive mill, where generations of the same family have cultivated and preserved the Itrana olive variety since 1860. Today, Itrana is considered one of the world's finest olive cultivars.

In Canneto Sabino, a hamlet of Fara in Sabina, in the province of Rieti, the 29th Festa dell'Olio Nuovo (New Olive Oil Festival) takes place on 7 and 8 November, under the theme Andar per olio e per cultura (Exploring Olive Oil and Culture).

The programme includes guided visits to Canneto's thousand-year-old olive tree and local mills, tasting courses dedicated to freshly pressed extra virgin olive oil, markets selling local produce, music and cultural tours.

Another initiative, Porta il tuo olio (Bring Your Own Oil), gives visitors the opportunity to have the acidity of their own olive oil tested free of charge and learn more about its characteristics.

In Tuscia, the arrival of the new season's olive oil is celebrated in Vignanello, in the province of Viterbo, with the 26th Festa dell'Olio e del Vino Novello (New Olive Oil and Wine Festival), running from 13 to 15 November.

Tastings, food trails and events exploring the world of extra virgin olive oil are combined with opportunities to discover the town's historic heritage, from Castello Ruspoli and its gardens to its ancient underground passages.

Two workshops are also scheduled for 8 and 15 November, both focusing on the role of high-quality extra virgin olive oil in the Mediterranean diet.

For anyone wishing to explore the world of extra virgin olive oil throughout the autumn, Villa Cavalletti in Grottaferrata, in the Castelli Romani hills, offers an experience combining history, landscape and flavour.

At this organic agricultural estate, the Olio et Amo experience includes a tour of the grounds and the Olive Oil Museum, an aroma workshop and a visit to the historic olive mill, where visitors can learn about traditional production methods.

The visit ends with a guided tasting of three olive oils, including a blind tasting designed to help participants identify a defective oil, followed by a final tasting served with bread made from organic flour produced on the estate.

Via Consolare Frasso, 5800 – 04010 Sonnino (LT)Tel. +39 0773 949008

items.title: Laura Pausini in Florence: “Music is queen, and I’m here to defend her”
items.summary: The Italian superstar takes the stage at Florence’s Mandela Forum today and tomorrow, with career-defining hits, lesser-known gems and a dazzling stage production
items.content:
Twenty years have passed since Laura Pausini made history by filling Milan's San Siro Stadium, becoming the first female artist ever to do so and bringing thousands of fans together in what felt like a celebratory ritual.

Today, she is the one travelling the world to meet them, with her Io Canto — Yo Canto World Tour 2026/27 , which has already sold a remarkable 450,000 tickets. The tour kicked off in Pamplona last March before marking its way across the Americas and now brings Pausini to Florence's Nelson Mandela Forum today and tomorrow.

“This year, the tour opened in Spain, South America and the United States. Three uninterrupted months on the road, travelling around the world, gave me an incredible boost of energy,” Pausini says. “I couldn't wait to bring this show, which means so much to me, to Europe and, above all, to Italy. If it were up to me, I would live on stage. It's my natural habitat, and being close to my audience and reconnecting with them live, year after year, is an absolute necessity for me.”

The setlist will bring together some of the biggest hits from a career that officially began on 27 February 1993, when a young Pausini won the Sanremo Music Festival with La solitudine .

Among the songs featured are Tra te e il mare , Come se non fosse stato mai amore , Frasi a metà and Una storia che vale . The audience can also look forward to Vivimi , Simili , Le cose che vivi , Benvenuto , Primavera in anticipo , Il primo passo sulla luna , Un'emergenza d'amore and Resta in ascolto .

These are songs that have become part of the collective memory, thanks to their ability to mirror emotions and experiences that resonate with people's everyday lives. Perhaps this powerful sense of connection is one of the reasons why Pausini is the most-streamed female Italian artist in the world.

One of the concert's highlights will be a medley paying tribute to fellow Italian artists, including Renato Zero, Gino Paoli, Umberto Tozzi and Ornella Vanoni.

Joining Laura on stage will be a seven-piece band and five backing vocalists, under the musical direction of Paolo Carta. This marks his eighth time taking on the role for one of the singer's world tours.

“Putting the setlist together means respecting the balance of my repertoire while following the story of my career in every country that has accompanied me over the years,” explains the artist, who has sold more than 75 million records worldwide and amassed over eight billion streams. “The European leg features many of my greatest hits, but also plenty of songs that may be less familiar to the general public but are much loved by my fans. These are the tracks they ask me to perform, and I love alternating them throughout the show.”

Pausini will also bring material from Io Canto 2/Yo Canto 2 , her tribute album celebrating the artists and songwriters who have shaped Italian music history, released last March.

The Spanish-language edition of the project, dedicated to Latin American singer-songwriters, has recently earned Pausini her 12th Latin Grammy nomination.

On 12 November, her album will compete in the Best Traditional Pop Vocal Album category ( Mejor Álbum Vocal Pop Tradicional ). The nomination comes three years after the Latin Recording Academy named her 2023 Latin Grammy Person of the Year, making her the first and only non-native Spanish-speaking artist to receive the honour.

Her connection with South America, after all, has become an inseparable part of her artistic journey.

“I'm thrilled by the affection and recognition that the Latin and American worlds have shown me for more than 30 years. Every time a nomination comes along, it feels different. You can never take it for granted.”

The stage production plays a central role in the show, conceived by Pausini together with her trusted creative collaborator Luca Tommasini.

The underlying idea was to create a luminous fortress: a protective space for music, with Laura taking on the role of a warrior who defends it, celebrates it and shares it with her audience. All materials used for the special effects are environmentally sustainable.

The entire show, organised and produced by Friends&Partners, has been meticulously planned to give each segment its own significance.

“The stage is our land, our fortress. The microphone stand is an extension of my muscles and of my voice. The microphone is my challenge, your voice, our megaphone. In this castle, I am not the queen: music is the queen, and I am here to defend her,” the singer declares at the opening of the show.

As she has done throughout her career, Pausini is also using this tour to keep the spotlight on violence against women. A longtime supporter of the Una Nessuna Centomila foundation, she has dedicated a special segment of the show to the issue, centred on Io sì , the song that earned her an Academy Award nomination and a Golden Globe.

“Violence is a silent scream disguised as love. It feeds on silence and leaves broken wings behind. It can only be defeated when no one is left invisible,” she says.

items.title: Europe takes notice: the secret behind Gattuso’s Lazio
items.summary: With 28 points from ten matches, Lazio have the best points-per-game record across Europe's five major leagues, ahead of Barcelona and Arsenal, and sit alone at the top of Serie A
items.content:
ROME — The element of surprise has gone. Europe has discovered Gennaro Gattuso's Lazio, and now everyone is studying how they do it. The statistics are remarkable: across Europe's five major football leagues, no team has a better points-per-game average than Lazio, who have collected 28 points from ten matches. Not even Barcelona or Arsenal can match the Biancocelesti's 2.8 points per game.

“As a manager, I'm not used to being up there,” Gattuso says with a smile.

A former defensive midfielder in Carlo Ancelotti's AC Milan side, he won everything alongside Andrea Pirlo in the Rossoneri shirt before lifting the World Cup with Italy in 2006.

But the World Cup became his curse as a manager. Appointed to replace Luciano Spalletti in the summer of 2025, he failed to guide Italy to the tournament in North America. Defeat to Bosnia in the play-off in Zenica meant a third consecutive World Cup absence for the Azzurri, a devastating blow for Gattuso personally.

Now, however, he sits alone at the top of the Italian league. It is a welcome feeling, and a relief too, after the suffocating loneliness of recent months.

First came the long walks in Marbella, where he lives when he is not coaching, as he tried somehow to come to terms with the pain of Zenica. Then came the scepticism that greeted his arrival at Lazio.

“Sport is wonderful because when you fall, you immediately get the chance to pick yourself up again,” he says, reflecting on the trauma of his time with the national team. “The important thing is not to sink into depression, but to rely on the people who love you. I have my wife Monica. We've been together for 30 years, and she's always been there through the difficult times.”

Yet his arrival at Lazio was hardly reassuring. It was a case of going from one hell to another, with supporters staging an indefinite boycott in protest against club president Claudio Lotito, staying away from matches and leaving the stadium empty. Virtually every decision the president makes is met with opposition.

“Let's put our helmets on and get going,” were Gattuso's first words.

In truth, he needed a full suit of armour. But Gattuso has built up plenty of armour over a lifetime of challenges, from the grief of losing his sister Francesca in 2020, aged just 37 — “I'd give everything I have to spend even an hour with her” — to the frightening experience of developing an eye condition, myasthenia gravis, which he has managed with corticosteroids every day for the past 15 years.

And yet the skies over Formello, Lazio's training headquarters, are growing brighter by the day. Coaching his players offers an escape from life's real problems.

That was why he reprimanded Nuno Tavares, a player he believes is “good enough for Real Madrid”, in front of the entire squad.

It could have destroyed their relationship. Instead, it sparked a remarkable chemistry between Gattuso, the Portuguese full-back and the rest of the team.

“Gattuso has transformed us. We give everything for him on the pitch,” his players keep saying, from Davide Frattesi to Christos Mandas.

“I've learnt to listen to today's players. I lose my temper less than I used to. These days they're on their phones even when they're lying on the physiotherapist's treatment table. That's inconceivable to me. But there are some rules I won't compromise on: respect and punctuality.”

“Once, it was raining and the gate at Olgiata [the residential estate near Formello where he lives] wouldn't open. I had to climb over it and run like a madman to get to training on time.”

He embraces them at the end of every match. They have won nine of their first ten games and on Sunday will look to pull off another result away at Napoli.

The Gattuso method, developed with the close-knit coaching staff that has accompanied him since the start of his managerial career, is working.

It involves what he calls “invisible training”: rest days designed to allow players to recover from the demanding sessions at Formello, combined with aggressive, direct, forward-thinking football on the pitch.

The element of surprise may have disappeared. But Gattuso is no longer alone, and his Lazio are learning to dream.

items.title: I ricchi non vogliono schermi nelle scuole dei loro figli
items.summary: Nella Silicon valley, in California, chi sviluppa app e piattaforme paga rette altissime per istituti privati in cui queste tecnologie non entrano. Le scuole più povere, invece, ne dipendono sempre di più Leggi
items.content:
German Gil è un programmatore e passa gran parte del suo tempo davanti a uno schermo. Nel 2015 si è trasferito a San Francisco e da allora ha lavorato per diverse startup e grandi aziende del settore tecnologico, tra cui Netflix e GitHub.

Ma quando è arrivato il momento di scegliere la scuola per la figlia Victoria, Gil voleva che avesse un’esperienza diversa, in un ambiente in cui “una bambina possa semplicemente essere una bambina”.

Gil e la moglie hanno iscritto Victoria alla Waldorf, un istituto privato basato sulla pedagogia steineriana , che punta molto sul gioco a contatto con la natura. Oggi Victoria fa la quarta elementare e trascorre le ore a scuola lontana dagli schermi. Invece di studiare sui computer portatili Chromebook , nella sua classe si rilegano libri a mano.

Tutto questo, però, ha un costo piuttosto alto. La retta della Waldorf, che si trova nel ricco quartiere di Pacific Heights, ad appena tre chilometri dagli uffici del gigante dell’intelligenza artificiale (ia) Anthropic, è di quarantamila dollari all’anno per la classe dai cinque ai sei anni. Per le superiori si sale a sessantamila. Eppure, nonostante i prezzi, l’approccio dell’istituto è sempre più in voga.

Per quanto possa sembrare controintuitivo, negli ultimi anni molti lavoratori ben pagati della Silicon valley hanno speso cifre enormi per allontanare i loro figli dalle stesse piattaforme che contribuiscono a sviluppare. Le domande d’iscrizione alla Waldorf sono cresciute senza sosta. La direttrice, Lauren Smith, dice che buona parte dei genitori degli alunni della Waldorf lavora nel campo della tecnologia.

Nelle enclave tecnologiche della California, da Mountain View a San Mateo, i genitori vorrebbero che le scuole pubbliche, dove gli schermi in classe sono una presenza fissa, tornassero a concentrarsi sui rapporti umani, seguendo l’esempio della Waldorf. Le loro iniziative hanno spinto alcuni istituti a vietare l’uso degli smartphone e a ridurre i compiti e i test da fare usando il computer.

Mentre si moltiplicano le prove dei danni che i social media e le piattaforme online causano alla crescita (anche i tribunali hanno cominciato a intervenire ), le famiglie e i governi locali stanno rivalutando il rapporto tra i ragazzi e la tecnologia, riflettendo sul ruolo dei dispositivi nell’apprendimento.

Di recente diversi grandi distretti scolastici, come quelli di New York City e Los Angeles, hanno deciso di limitare il ricorso alla tecnologia. Anche in altri paesi del mondo i genitori sono più critici nei confronti dell’uso dei dispositivi.

“Oggi si parla molto di più di questi argomenti rispetto a qualche anno fa”, conferma David Monahan, direttore delle campagne di Fairplay, un’organizzazione statunitense che si batte per limitare l’uso degli schermi tra bambini e bambine.

I genitori della Silicon valley offrono qualcosa in più rispetto ad altre comunità: la conoscenza diretta del settore. Quando l’anno scorso il distretto che riunisce le superiori di San Mateo ha creato una squadra per valutare che conseguenze può avere l’uso dell’ia in classe, almeno due dei componenti lavoravano per grandi aziende tecnologiche, tra cui la sezione di Google che si occupa proprio d’ia, come ha confermato Jennifer Jacobson del consiglio scolastico.

“Rispetto ad altri, questi adulti conoscono meglio la tecnologia”, sottolinea Jacobson. “Sono in grado di prevederne gli sviluppi e il potenziale effetto sull’apprendimento”.

Molte famiglie statunitensi sono sbalordite quando scoprono il modo in cui gli schermi entrano nelle scuole. Jillian Kolongowski, scrittrice che vive a San Mateo, è rimasta senza parole vedendo la figlia di cinque anni tornare a casa con un Chromebook per fare gli esercizi di matematica. “Mi sono detta: ‘Che diavolo è quello? Va all’asilo!’”, racconta Kolongowski.

Candice Wei, una tutor di Palo Alto che aiuta ragazzi e ragazze delle superiori nell’ammissione al college, ha avuto una reazione simile quando ha scoperto che alla scuola dell’infanzia di suo figlio bambine e bambini usavano gli schermi in classe con restrizioni minime. Wei ha così deciso di capire quali fossero le regole applicate alle superiori. “YouTube non è vietato, così come l’ia generativa. È una scelta quasi criminale”, accusa. “Io non permetto che si usino a casa mia. Perché a scuola sì?”.

All’inizio il ricorso alla tecnologia nelle scuole era visto come il segno di un futuro digitale più giusto e accessibile. In molti casi i dispositivi elettronici, essenziali durante la pandemia per garantire le lezioni a distanza, non sono stati abbandonati dopo il ritorno in classe. Nel 2025 il 99 per cento degli insegnanti che avevano partecipato a un sondaggio del New York Times riferiva che i loro studenti avevano ricevuto dispositivi direttamente dalle scuole, mentre l’81 per cento riferiva che i bambini entravano in contatto con gli schermi già a cinque anni.

Oggi gli esperti e un numero crescente di genitori temono l’onnipresenza della tecnologia. Metà degli adolescenti statunitensi trascorre almeno quattro ore al giorno davanti a uno schermo, senza contare il tempo in cui usa i dispositivi per le attività scolastiche. Monahan pensa che la presenza degli schermi in classe non faccia altro che rafforzare queste tendenze. “Che tipo di abitudini promuoviamo a scuola, se ragazzi e ragazze passano ore a fissare gli schermi con l’approvazione dei loro insegnanti?”, si domanda.

Diverse ricerche mostrano che gli studenti memorizzano meglio usando carta e penna invece che uno schermo. Altri sottolineano che l’uso eccessivo dei dispositivi ostacola il legame tra studente e insegnante, un aspetto fondamentale per la crescita emotiva. Inoltre, elimina quello sforzo che favorisce l’apprendimento.

“Le persone sono molto più propense a impegnarsi per un insegnante o un genitore che per un computer, che non ricambierà mai il loro affetto”, spiega Yvonne Kao, dell’organizzazione WestEd, specializzata in istruzione.

Kao nota che negli Stati Uniti l’uso della tecnologia cambia molto tra i diversi distretti scolastici. E racconta di aver sentito parlare di aree rurali in cui non c’è personale in grado di valutare correttamente le diverse tecnologie e abbastanza aggiornato da capire cosa conviene comprare.

I genitori della Silicon valley sono in una posizione diversa. “Hanno una dimestichezza che, credo, si acquisisce solo vivendo immersi in quell’ambiente”, aggiunge Kao. “Sanno cos’è utile e cos’è dannoso, quindi possono provare a trovare un giusto equilibrio”.

La diffusione degli schermi nelle scuole pubbliche ha spinto molte famiglie tra le braccia degli istituti privati. Libere dalla burocrazia locale e statale, le scuole private della California possono cambiare strada più velocemente e introdurre limiti, oltre ad avere più risorse per pagare gli insegnanti invece di affidarsi alle app.

Wei ha aperto la sede locale dell’organizzazione Schools beyond screens ed è convinta che il ricorso agli schermi in classe sia uno dei principali motivi per cui i genitori decidono di abbandonare la scuola pubblica. “Sono stata contattata da persone che hanno preso in considerazione una scuola pubblica per i loro figli, l’hanno visitata, hanno visto studenti incollati agli schermi e hanno pensato: ‘Beh, meglio andare nelle private’”, racconta.

Questa situazione ha spinto Wei e altri a fare pressione sui distretti scolastici perché verifichino le credenziali delle aziende che ottengono appalti milionari con le scuole ed esigano prove solide sulla capacità dei loro prodotti di migliorare l’apprendimento. “Significa chiedere dati precisi sui risultati che si aspettano di ottenere, e sapere qual è il piano nel caso in cui non li raggiungano”, dice Kolongowski, il cui marito lavora nel campo dell’intelligenza artificiale. “Molte aziende del settore pubblicizzano soluzioni davvero allettanti, ma poi i risultati non sono all’altezza delle aspettative”.

Grazie alle pressioni delle famiglie, le scuole pubbliche di San Mateo hanno smesso di distribuire portatili ai bambini fino alla seconda elementare. Gli studenti delle superiori, invece, hanno il divieto assoluto di usare i telefoni. A Mountain View le scuole stanno smettendo di usare i-Ready, una piattaforma per la lettura e lo studio della matematica usata nei distretti scolastici californiani, criticata per le lezioni ripetitive e accusata di condividere i dati personali degli studenti senza il loro consenso.

Intanto le scuole pubbliche di Palo Alto hanno vietato l’uso di un prodotto tecnologico creato a pochi chilometri di distanza: gli occhiali smart .

I sostenitori dell’apprendimento centrato sulla persona sono soddisfatti di questi progressi, ma temono che i distretti con meno risorse rimangano indietro, e siano costretti a usare gli strumenti tecnologici che le scuole più ricche stanno abbandonando.

L’ostilità nei confronti della tecnologia in classe è un fenomeno molto diffuso, sottolinea Jon Valant, direttore del centro di ricerca sulle politiche scolastiche della Brookings institution. A prescindere dal reddito, i genitori vogliono la stessa cosa per i figli: un’istruzione di alta qualità e basata sui rapporti umani. La differenza è che alcuni possono permettersela, mentre altri no.
